A.biggest_strength: Two-phase step animation on the array that separates comparing mid (with an inline inequality like 34 < 37) from dropping the eliminated half (with an explicit "dropped 8" bracket and smoothly sliding low/high pointers), aligned directly above a spatial range ladder.
A.biggest_weakness: Severe SVG text collision at 390px mobile width in Scene 5 ("MOST COMPARES FOR N SORTED CELLS" overlaps "×1,000 cells: +10 compares"), combined with a static log2(n) scene where the headline equation k <= log2(n) disagrees with the 5-compare bar for n = 16 and array cells cannot be clicked.
factual_errors: In Scene 5 ("Why log₂ n"), the displayed headline equation is n / 2^k >= 1 => k <= log₂ n, which for n = 16 gives k <= 4, directly disagreeing with the bar chart immediately below it ("n = 16: 5") and the scene text ("so 16 cells need at most 5 compares"); the +1 needed for the final 1-cell check (⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1 = 5) is omitted from the equation and only appears in the small corner readout and bottom notes.

When searching for a missing target (e.g., 40, 15, or 0), at the final step where low > high and 0 cells remain in the array, the "RANGE AT EACH COMPARE" ladder still stops at row 4 showing "1 cell" and never shows the final empty range (0 cells).
At 390px mobile width in Scene 5, the SVG heading "MOST COMPARES FOR N SORTED CELLS" and the annotation "×1,000 cells: +10 compares" overlap and render on top of each other.
A.interaction_feedback: What worked: The preset buttons (37 found, 79 most compares, 40 missing), the live target number input (which updates immediately on input without needing Enter), the < and > step buttons, the step range slider, and keyboard controls (Left/Right arrows for scenes, Up/Down arrows and comma/period for steps, Tab/Enter on buttons) all responded smoothly, and --reduced motion cleanly skipped the animated sweep in Scene 4. What broke or confused: Clicking Scene 4 ("4 Close in") flashes the final completed step (step 7) for 500ms before resetting to step 0 to start an 8-second beat animation. The 5 scene buttons and the 8-step scrubber are awkwardly coupled because Scenes 1–4 are mapped to steps 0, 1, 2, and last() of the same trace, so touching the step slider or target input while in Scene 5 yanks the reader out of Scene 5 back to an earlier scene. At 390px mobile width, scene button labels disappear (leaving only tiny numbers 1–5), the TARGET box moves to an odd spot below the high pointer and vanishes in Scene 5, and Scene 5's SVG text collides. What a reader would want to do but cannot: Click directly on a cell in the array to search for its value, or interactively vary the array size n in the "Why log₂ n" view.

B.biggest_strength: Two cohesive, complementary interactive figures that pair a 32-element clickable array (with live-highlighted code and a candidate-range funnel showing exact counts vs. theoretical bounds) with an interactive log-scale array-size slider (n = 1 to 1,000,000,000) that dynamically renders the entire halving ladder.
B.biggest_weakness: Each comparison step in the first figure renders the array pointers (lo and hi) in their post-comparison updated positions on the same screen as the mid element just compared, so mid appears outside the active [lo, hi] range and the lo/hi tags disappear completely when lo > hi on a missing target; additionally, the Find input uses onchange rather than oninput.
factual_errors: While all numbers and formulas are mathematically accurate, in Figure 1 each step k displays the comparison at mid = tr[k-1].mid alongside the already-updated range [lo, hi] = rangeAfter(k), so the visual lo/hi tags on the array disagree with the pre-comparison (lo + hi) // 2 values described in the step text (e.g., at Comparison 1, the text computes mid = (0 + 31) // 2 = 15, while the array already places the lo tag at index 16 to the right of mid; and on the final step of a missing search when lo > hi, both lo and hi tags disappear from the array).
B.interaction_feedback: What worked: Clicking any of the 32 array cells immediately starts a search for that cell's value; Step, Back, Play/Pause, and Reset buttons work cleanly with appropriate disabled states; live code highlighting and the candidate funnel (with purple split pips and theoretical bounds) update in lockstep; keyboard shortcuts (ArrowRight, ArrowLeft, R, Tab, Enter) work well; the Figure 2 log-scale slider smoothly updates n from 1 to 1,000,000,000 along with the linear/binary comparison counts, speedup ratio, and scaled halving ladder; and the 390px mobile layout reflows the 32 cells into a clean 4x8 grid with zero text collisions. What broke or confused: Typing a custom number into the Find input (#target) does not update the figure until the reader presses Enter or blurs the input because it listens to onchange instead of oninput. Also, combining the mid comparison and the lo/hi pointer update into a single step means you never see mid inside the [lo, hi] bracket being halved, and when lo > hi on a missing target, the lo and hi tags vanish instead of visibly crossing. What a reader would want to do but cannot: Drag a step scrubber to jump to a specific comparison in Figure 1, click a one-click preset button for a missing value in Figure 1, or see an intermediate "before drop" vs. "after drop" state for each comparison.

structured_output.reasons: Page B better serves a blog post reader for both halves of the request. In Figure 1, Page B lets the reader click any of 32 array cells (or enter any value), steps through the search while highlighting the exact line of code executed, and builds a spatial funnel comparing actual candidates left against the theoretical n/2^k bound. In Figure 2, Page B clearly derives the worst-case bound ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1 and provides an interactive log-scale slider (from n = 1 to 1 billion) that dynamically draws the halving ladder, whereas Page A's log₂ n scene is a static 4-bar chart whose headline equation (k <= log₂ n) omits the +1 (contradicting the 5-compare bar for n = 16) and suffers from severe SVG text overlap at 390px mobile width.
